claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations and heterogeneous microstructures.
A transformer model can directly use preprocessed SEM/XRD images, chemical-fluctuation descriptors, and mechanical-test data to predict mechanical properties of HfNbTiVAl10.
Only a limited or minimal tensile and fracture dataset will be sufficient for the proposed model.
The proposed model will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness.
The proposed model will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 10–15% over conventional simulation and standard machine-learning methods.
The proposed model will increase R² from approximately 0.85 to approximately 0.97.
The proposed model will be approximately 100 times more computationally efficient than conventional simulation methods.
The model's embedded features will capture multilevel chemical fluctuations and hierarchical microstructural heterogeneity.
Transformer self-attention will capture both local and long-range microstructural correlations.
Learning correlations between heterogeneous chemical features and macroscopic mechanical responses will enable prediction of fracture toughness.
Replacing full-scale simulations with transformer inference will drastically reduce computational requirements.
CALPHAD, first-principles calculations, and standard machine learning require high computational resources.
Conventional methods have limited accuracy, particularly for predicting fracture toughness.
The model is intended to be valid from ambient to moderately elevated temperatures represented in its training data.
Degraded input-image quality will reduce model reliability.
Descriptors that do not accurately represent the hierarchical structure will reduce model reliability.
Insufficient imaging resolution or imaging that is unsynchronized with mechanical testing will make the model unreliable.
Operation outside the temperature range represented by the training data will make the model unreliable.
The estimated accuracy and efficiency gains are based on existing transformer applications in materials science.
A blinded prospective benchmark on new HfNbTiVAl10 specimens can compare model predictions with measured Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.
